executive_summary: The dominant connecting thread across today's content is the global contest over power, legitimacy, and who controls the rules of major institutions — from politics to sports to technology. The Atlantic's in-depth analysis of masculinism identifies it as a coordinated ideological movement functioning as the connective tissue of the American right, explicitly aimed at reversing women's institutional gains; this pairs directly with Foreign Affairs' examination of Orbán's fall and Europe's political realignment, both of which reflect a broader struggle over who sets the terms of governance in democratic societies. The Athletic's coverage of the WNBA's officiating problem and the College Football Playoff expansion further illustrates how institutional credibility and rule-making authority are under pressure across arenas — who referees the game, and whether those referees are trusted, has become a defining question. MIT Technology Review's account of Musk's failed suit against OpenAI adds a corporate dimension to the same theme: powerful actors are increasingly willing to use legal and political mechanisms to challenge institutions they cannot control. Taken together, today's content tells a single story about legitimacy under siege — the rules, norms, and bodies that once governed major domains of public life are being openly contested from multiple directions simultaneously.

That was Victor Wembanyama's stat line from the Spurs' 122-115 double-overtime victory in Game 1 of the Western Conference finals last night. Since blocked shots started being recorded in the 1973-74 season, only three players have put up 40 points, 24 boards and three blocks in a playoff game. Over in Los Angeles, Sparks fans welcomed Caitlin Clark back to Crypto.com Arena for the first time since May of her rookie season, where she won her first-ever WNBA game.

longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism — a coordinated right-wing movement seeking to reverse women's legal, professional, and political gains — is not a legitimate response to male struggles but a misogynist ideology functioning as the ideological glue of the American right.
longform.context: The piece serves as a reader note accompanying The Atlantic's June 2026 cover story, prompted by the visible mainstreaming of masculinist figures and ideas within the contemporary American right, including figures connected to the Trump administration such as Pete Hegseth.
arguments: Masculinism is a coherent political movement, not a fringe — its proponents include Douglas Wilson (who counts Hegseth as a denominational member), Raw Egg Nationalist (Charles Cornish-Dale), and Helen Andrews, each advancing distinct but reinforcing claims: that feminism made women 'ugly and unhappy,' that low testosterone causes liberalism, and that female authority is 'a threat to civilization.'

Lewis acknowledges a legitimate factual core — that some men and boys face real, under-discussed struggles (citing male problem gambling as one example) — but argues this evidence does not validate the masculinists' broader causal claim that feminism has 'ruined America.'

Masculinism's central cultural target is empathy, which its proponents frame as a 'dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals,' revealing that the movement's gender politics are inseparable from its stances on immigration and criminal justice — making it a unifying ideological force rather than a narrowly gendered grievance.

The movement's explicit policy goals — repealing the Nineteenth Amendment, instituting a 'family wage,' reversing workplace integration — represent not nostalgia but an active program to return women to the legal and economic status they held in 1857, when The Atlantic was founded.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it reframes masculinism from a cultural curiosity into 'the single most important force holding together the American right,' a characterization with direct implications for understanding coalition politics in the Trump era. By tracing the movement's intellectual architecture through named figures with institutional and governmental connections, Lewis challenges the tendency to dismiss manosphere rhetoric as online noise. It also raises the question of whether acknowledging male struggles — as Lewis does — can be disentangled from masculinist political projects that exploit those struggles.
questions_raised: Lewis concedes that male struggles are real and under-addressed, but the piece does not resolve how to respond to those struggles without inadvertently legitimizing a masculinist framing — leaving open the question of what a non-masculinist politics of male welfare would look like.

The piece asserts masculinism is 'the single most important force holding together the American right' but, as a newsletter note rather than the full article, does not fully evidence this claim — leaving open whether the cover story substantiates it or whether this framing is itself contested.
